content: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is defined as a blood loss of 500 mL or more following childbirth and is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the routine administration of a prophylactic uterotonic agent to all women during childbirth to prevent PPH. Despite this preventive measure, PPH remains a significant complication, accounting for approximately one-quarter of all maternal deaths globally. When PPH occurs despite prophylaxis, the administration of uterotonic agents as first-line treatment is recommended. However, there is uncertainty regarding which uterotonic agent is the most effective and safest for first-line treatment. The objective of this study was to identify the most effective uterotonic agent(s) with the least side effects for the treatment of PPH and to establish a meaningful ranking of available agents based on their relative efficacy and safety profiles. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth's Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to May 5, 2020. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. Randomized controlled trials and cluster-randomized trials comparing the effectiveness and safety of different uterotonic agents for PPH treatment were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The primary outcomes were additional blood loss of 500 mL or more after trial recruitment until cessation of active bleeding and a composite outcome of maternal death or severe morbidity. Secondary outcomes included other blood loss-related outcomes, morbidity outcomes, and patient-reported outcomes. Pairwise meta-analyses and indirect comparisons were performed where possible, but a planned network meta-analysis could not be conducted due to the limited number of studies. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of the evidence. Seven trials involving 3,738 women across 10 countries were included in the review. All trials were conducted in hospital settings, and most participants gave birth vaginally, except for one small trial that included both vaginal and cesarean deliveries. The uterotonic agents evaluated included oxytocin alone (six trial arms), misoprostol plus oxytocin (four trial arms), misoprostol alone (three trial arms), and Syntometrine® (a fixed-dose combination of oxytocin and ergometrine) plus oxytocin infusion (one trial arm). A pairwise meta-analysis of two trials (1,787 participants) suggested that misoprostol, when used as a first-line uterotonic agent, probably increases the risk of requiring a blood transfusion compared to oxytocin (risk ratio [RR] 1.47, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02 to 2.14, moderate-certainty evidence). Low-certainty evidence indicated that misoprostol might increase the likelihood of additional blood loss of 1,000 mL or more (RR 2.57, 95% CI 1.00 to 6.64). The data comparing misoprostol to oxytocin were imprecise for outcomes such as additional blood loss of 500 mL or more (RR 1.66, 95% CI 0.69 to 4.02, low-certainty), maternal death or severe morbidity (RR 1.98, 95% CI 0.36 to 10.72, low-certainty), and the need for additional uterotonics (RR 1.30, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.94, low-certainty). Misoprostol was associated with an increased risk of side effects, including vomiting (RR 2.47, 95% CI 1.37 to 4.47, high-certainty) and fever (RR 3.43, 95% CI 0.65 to 18.18, low-certainty). A pairwise meta-analysis of four trials (1,881 participants) provided high-certainty evidence that the combination of misoprostol and oxytocin made little or no difference in the need for additional uterotonics (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.05) or blood transfusion (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17) compared to oxytocin alone. The combination may offer a potential benefit for reducing additional blood loss of 500 mL or more (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.06, moderate-certainty) and 1,000 mL or more (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.34, moderate-certainty), but the evidence is not definitive. The combination was associated with an increased risk of fever (RR 3.07, 95% CI 2.62 to 3.61, high-certainty) and vomiting (RR 1.85, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.95, high-certainty) compared to oxytocin alone. The evidence comparing misoprostol to the combination of Syntometrine® and oxytocin was of very low certainty, leaving the effects unclear. Indirect comparisons suggested that the combination of misoprostol and oxytocin probably reduces the risk of blood transfusion (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.99, moderate-certainty) and may reduce the risk of additional blood loss of 1,000 mL or more (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.89, low-certainty) compared to misoprostol alone. The combination made little or no difference in the risk of vomiting (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.59, high-certainty) compared to misoprostol alone. However, the effects on other outcomes, such as additional blood loss of 500 mL or more, maternal mortality or severe morbidity, the need for additional uterotonics, and fever, were uncertain due to low-certainty evidence. In conclusion, the available evidence suggests that oxytocin is likely more effective and associated with fewer side effects than misoprostol when used as a first-line treatment for PPH. Adding misoprostol to oxytocin may not significantly improve effectiveness outcomes and is associated with an increased risk of side effects. The evidence for other commonly used uterotonic agents, such as injectable prostaglandins, ergometrine, and Syntometrine®, is limited or absent.
